question: How should the commons choose its words?
found: Domain-driven design keeps one ubiquitous language used the same way in talk, code and documents - a word with two meanings is a bug. Orwell and the plain-language guidelines ask for the short everyday word a reader already knows, one term for one thing, and no jargon where an everyday word will do. So: look at what others call the thing and what the reader knows, prefer the plain word, keep one meaning, and record the words rejected.

question: How should code be changed so an edit cannot silently miss?
found: Text patches break on formatting: nineteen times a pattern written for one layout met another. Structural tools (ast-grep on tree-sitter, Comby, rust-analyzer's replace) match code as code. Tried on a real bug: ast-grep matched a whole function by its signature and replaced it; it did not see an expression inside a write! macro, because macro insides are tokens. So: replace whole items, keep logic outside macros, put new views in new files, and let every edit stop the job when it does not take.

question: How do people measure repetitive manual work and how draining it is, and decide when to automate it?
found: Site reliability engineering names it toil - manual, repetitive, automatable, without enduring value - and keeps it within a budget. Perceived exertion is rated on one 0-10 scale (Borg CR10); workload can be split into six parts (NASA-TLX), too heavy for every record. Whether automation pays is time per occurrence times frequency (xkcd 1205). Toyota's jidoka makes the machine judge and stop itself, so no person stands by to judge.

question: Read as a database, how sound is ocoeco's data?
found: Measured 2026-11-12 across 22 projects: 14 tables; about 860 links between rows written as text (research 143, sources 317, decided 75, advances 88, touches 104, serves 129, answers 1), of which 2 point at an id found nowhere. Sound in practice, but held together by discipline: no relation is declared, so nothing checks one. Read with tad sql, each project's data already answers joins; what is missing is the shared language saying which field refers to which table, and a check across projects.

question: Does open source have the intelligence and analysis a business has?
found: From the outside, yes: CHAOSS (the Linux Foundation, since 2017) defines metrics of activity and health, and GrimoireLab and Augur gather them from commits, issues, reviews and mailing lists. From the inside, no: why things are as they are, what was decided and rejected, what is needed next, who is doing it, and a way for the people who use the software to see that and take part. That inside is the analysis half of business intelligence and analysis; it is what ocoeco records as the work's own data, oco-agent coordinates, and the observatory presents.

question: How do tables serve the commons today, do they do something a graph of the best kind cannot, and how has the world dealt with what we are dealing with?
found: Looked at ourselves first (2026-11-13). Of 36 parts in the lenses built in: 14 only filter the rows of one kind; 15 count or gather; 9 bring two kinds together; 8 take a name apart to find what it points at; 1 is placed. All 22 tables are declared as a minimum - a row may carry more - and all are keyed by id alone: they are kinds of thing with an id, not tables in the strict sense. And the work about what bears on what is done outside any table: 280 lines of the program check links, 473 rewrite them when rows move, 59 walk a chain. So tables serve us for counting and gathering, for a whole thing readable on one line, and for checks when written; they do not give identity, edges, walking, what points at a thing, or what was. In the world: a table is one way of sorting facts, not the facts - Datomic keeps facts and answers row-like and column-like questions from the same ones; identity can be what a thing is, with names as labels (Unison); a graph can be declared over tables that exist and walked in the engine we use (SQL/PGQ); and text at rest with a graph when asked is a working arrangement (Logseq), whose newer form warns against giving up the text. In power a table does nothing a graph of facts cannot; in practice it gives a mature, fast engine and a row a person can read whole. The middle man is at the asking, not at rest: at rest we already keep things with ids and links - nodes and edges, written as text.

question: What should the board be, taking the best the world has?
found: Kanban (Anderson, from Toyota's production system): make the flow visible, limit work in progress, pull, make policies explicit, measure time. Reinertsen: queues and ageing are the hidden cost. GitHub Projects and Linear: an item is kept once, with fields, and seen through many views - a board is a view, never a second list. Shape Up's hill charts: show uncertainty, not only state. For OCO: the board is a view over every project's backlog - one truth, the data the work already keeps - with the flow open, next, in-progress, waiting, parked, done, dropped; each item in progress held by a driver, with its next step and the day it entered its state; and what needs attention said plainly: a driver holding too much, work with no next step, work that has not moved for a week. oco-agent speaks it; anyone - a person or a machine - pulls from next. Not yet: uncertainty (hill charts), and what someone outside could pick up.

question: Lens by lens, what does the best of the world's experience say - stripped of ceremony - and what does ocoeco keep or lack for it?
found: PURPOSE - best: say why a thing exists and what it must reach in terms that can be checked, and few of them. Keeps: the idea, milestones with criteria and readiness. Lacks: nothing essential. KNOWLEDGE - best: every claim with its source, and a question before an answer. Keeps: research, sources, concepts, vocabulary. Lacks: how a finding is known - measured, read, or reasoned; on 2026-11-12 a reasoned guess (a request with no time limit) stood beside measured facts and was wrong. REASONING - best: a decision on one page with its context, what was rejected, its consequences and its status (Toyota's A3, Nygard's decision records). Keeps: decisions with why, rejected, research, sources. Lacks: the relation between decisions - one refining or replacing another is written as text today, three times on 2026-11-12. WORK - best: visible flow, pull, limits, ageing (Kanban, Reinertsen). Keeps: the backlog's flow, driver, next, since, waits_on; oco-agent's journal says what actually ran. Lacks: why this work - its link to the milestone or decision it serves. RESULTS - best: evidence that can be checked, not a claim. Keeps: glimpses, workings with evidence, gathered releases, activity and test runs. Lacks: evidence as a link to the thing that proves it. LOOKING BACK - best: the After Action Review, hansei. Keeps: reflections. Lacks: nothing essential. PROBLEMS - best: the andon - a problem visible the moment it happens, to everyone, until it is dealt with. Keeps: nothing of its own; attention is computed for the flow only. Lacks: the lens itself - 21 release runs failed unseen and a watcher was silent for a night on 2026-11-12. The largest gap. INVITATION - best: a need marked where it is, small and well-defined, fillable by whoever passes (Wikipedia's citation needed, good-first-issue labels, citizen science, device owners filling a support table). Keeps: nothing. Lacks: the entity - what is needed, of what kind (information, a test on a device, feedback), where, and how to give it. What open commons add to Toyota's room. THE SKY ITSELF - what makes lenses one dome: relations seen as connections, the story, and time. Keeps: about 860 links that resolve, the essence a star tells, and history in git. Lacks: the relations declared - the dome's continuity rests on them. So, in order: declare the relations (among them one decision refining another, and work serving a milestone); the problems lens; the invitation; how a finding is known and evidence that links; then lenses as data.
sources: obeya, kanban-anderson, product-development-flow, adr-nygard, toyota-production-system, citation-needed, zooniverse, after-action-review, ostrom-commons

question: What is a board, taking the best of the world's experience and leaving its ceremony out - and what is it for open commons?
found: The best of it is Toyota's obeya, the big room: begun on the Prius project because no single person held the knowledge the work needed, its walls showed purpose, plan, progress, problems and countermeasures together, so that anyone entering saw the whole and problems became visible. Around it: make things visible (mieruka), signal a problem at once (andon), go and see the real thing, pull work rather than push it, a decision on one page with its reasoning (A3), and look back (hansei). What was added later - command centres, score boards, points, ceremonies - is the part to leave out. A board, then, is not a list of tasks: it is the room, and a flow of work is one of its walls. ocoeco's entities already are those walls: the idea and milestones (purpose); research, sources, concepts and words (knowledge); decisions with what was rejected (reasoning); the backlog's flow (work); glimpses, workings and their evidence (results); reflections (looking back); what needs attention (problems). Open commons need one wall Toyota's room never did: there nobody is assigned, so the room must also invite - show what is needed from whoever comes: a piece of information, a test on a device, feedback. Ostrom found commons last where those who use a thing can see its state and take part in its rules.

question: How should the data about work be produced so it cannot go stale, and can ocoeco take over what release-please and release-plz do?
found: Measured 2026-11-11: only 224 of 464 recent landed commits across 22 projects (48%) changed any ocoeco data - half of all work leaves no trace in the system. 7 projects use release-please or release-plz; what anything consumes from them is the version and the tag (the conveyor builds binaries from tags, update-pins reads them, crates.io publishing hangs off them); their changelogs (23 to 470 lines of commit titles) drive nothing. Prior art: changesets and Knope record a change's intent when it is made and consume it at release (highest bump wins), but their record is only a bump and a summary, tied to nothing else. Git documents that local hooks can be bypassed (--no-verify); the guarantee has to be at the boundary that cannot be skipped - CI on the pull request, and land.
sources: changesets, knope, githooks, git-trailers, release-please, release-plz

question: What does a lens do with what passes through it - what is its second face called?
found: The author, 2026-11-12: a lens propagates light, it lets it through; by itself it shows nothing - it is not a screen or a picture - and the word showing falls off the full picture, as if from another domain. In optics a lens is defined by this: it transmits light and brings it to a focus; a telescope's lens gathers a star's faint light and focuses it, so that a blur becomes something one can make out. So the second face of a lens is its focus, and the act is to focus. It is plain and can be guessed (focus the lens on a star); it says the true thing about the data - nothing is made, the same data is brought into focus; and it leaves the showing where it happens, on the fulldome. The whole then reads as one picture: a star gives off light, its data; a glimpse catches it where it is fresh; a lens lets it through and brings it into focus; the fulldome is where it is seen; to observe is to gather the light of many stars. Shine is no act of ocoeco: it is what a star does by working.

question: What should one recorded look at work be called, in the observatory's language?
found: Observatories keep an observing log; each look is an observation, recorded with its time, target, observer and notes, written at the eyepiece while fresh, and entries point to what they relate to. Weighed: snapshot (already a filesystem and VM word in the author's world - two meanings), exposure (also risk), frame (overloaded in software), observation (exact but long, and it blurs with what the observatory itself does), sighting (seeing someone else's object), entry (says nothing). glimpse: plain, short, one meaning here, and honest that each look is partial - together they make the picture.

question: What should a look back over a stretch of work be called, and what should it hold?
found: The author's word, 2026-11-12, is reflection. Schon showed practitioners learn by reflecting on action; the US Army's After Action Review asks what was planned, what happened, why, and what next; Agile retrospectives are a team ceremony at an iteration's end; blameless postmortems are written after failures. ocoeco needs the plain, general one: anyone - a person or a machine - looking back over any stretch, at any time, about success or failure, saying what they saw, what they learned and what changes.

question: What should ocoeco's three acts be called?
found: The author proposed, 2026-11-12: pulse for record (a pulsating star), shine for show, observe for observe. Observe is plain, belongs with star and observatory, and replaces harvest and discover - a farm's word and a search's. Pulse is taken: since 2026-11-12 it means oco-agent's sign of life to the switch outside, and beat a driver's; and someone typing it could not guess it writes a row, where record can be guessed. Shine reads two ways: in everyday speech a star that shines can be seen (show); in the sky what a star shines is its light, which here is its data (record). A word that can be read as either of two acts will be. Better to touch the act first - build one lens, run it - and name it then. Resolved the same day by the author: the act called record already had its word - glimpse (2026-11-11). A glimpse is the part of a lens that takes data in; so the three acts are glimpse, observe and show.
